claim: MEK1 was required to make Xenopus pluripotent cells competent to respond to all cell fate inducers tested.
source: MEK1 was required to make Xenopus pluripotent cells competent to respond to all cell fate inducers tested.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MEK1 activity was necessary to clear the pluripotency protein Ventx2 at the onset of gastrulation.
source: Importantly, MEK1 activity was necessary to clear the pluripotency protein Ventx2 at the onset of gastrulation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data showing Ventx2 persistence in MEK1 morphants.

claim: Concomitant MEK1 and Ventx2 knockdown restored the competence of embryonic cells to differentiate.
source: Thus, concomitant MEK1 and Ventx2 knockdown restored the competence of embryonic cells to differentiate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments showing restored marker expression and morphogenesis in double morphants.

claim: MEK1 appeared to control the asymmetric inheritance of Ventx2 protein following cell division.
source: Strikingly, MEK1 appeared to control the asymmetric inheritance of Ventx2 protein following cell division.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data showing asymmetric Ventx2 distribution in dividing cells.

claim: When Ventx2 lacked a functional PEST-destruction motif, it was stabilized.
source: Consistently, when Ventx2 lacked a functional PEST-destruction motif, it was stabilized, displayed symmetric distribution during cell division and could efficiently maintain pluripotency gene expression over time.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with 2SAVentx2-Myc showing increased nuclear presence and persistence.

claim: When Ventx2 lacked a functional PEST-destruction motif, it displayed symmetric distribution during cell division.
source: Consistently, when Ventx2 lacked a functional PEST-destruction motif, it was stabilized, displayed symmetric distribution during cell division and could efficiently maintain pluripotency gene expression over time.
evidence: This is shown by quantification of Myc signal intensity ratios between daughter nuclei.

claim: When Ventx2 lacked a functional PEST-destruction motif, it could efficiently maintain pluripotency gene expression over time.
source: Consistently, when Ventx2 lacked a functional PEST-destruction motif, it was stabilized, displayed symmetric distribution during cell division and could efficiently maintain pluripotency gene expression over time.
evidence: This is supported by WISH data showing sustained pou5f3.2 expression in 2SAVentx2 injected embryos.

claim: In mammals, epiblast cells of the developing blastula embryo transit through a series of pluripotent states until gastrulation.
source: In mammals, epiblast cells of the developing blastula embryo appear to transit through a series of pluripotent states until gastrulation, which signs the global extinction of pluripotency and the rise of cell competence to somatically commit (Hackett and Surani, 2014; Boroviak and Nichols, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gastrulation signs the global extinction of pluripotency and the rise of cell competence to somatically commit in mammals.
source: In mammals, epiblast cells of the developing blastula embryo appear to transit through a series of pluripotent states until gastrulation, which signs the global extinction of pluripotency and the rise of cell competence to somatically commit (Hackett and Surani, 2014; Boroviak and Nichols, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In amphibians, cells of the blastula animal hemisphere are somatically pluripotent.
source: In amphibians, cells of the blastula animal hemisphere are somatically pluripotent, and their broad potential is globally lost at gastrulation (Snape et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The broad potential of amphibian blastula animal hemisphere cells is globally lost at gastrulation.
source: In amphibians, cells of the blastula animal hemisphere are somatically pluripotent, and their broad potential is globally lost at gastrulation (Snape et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Pou-V members Pou5f3 and Pou5f1 share functional homology in regulating the uncommitted state of progenitor cells.
source: Pou-V members Pou5f3 and Pou5f1 share functional homology in regulating the uncommitted state of progenitor cells (Livigni et al., 2013) and in reprogramming somatic cells to induced-Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs) (Tapia et al., 2012; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pou-V members Pou5f3 and Pou5f1 share functional homology in reprogramming somatic cells to induced-Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs).
source: Pou-V members Pou5f3 and Pou5f1 share functional homology in regulating the uncommitted state of progenitor cells (Livigni et al., 2013) and in reprogramming somatic cells to induced-Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs) (Tapia et al., 2012; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Nanog gene is absent in the Xenopus genus.
source: Nonetheless, phylogenetic, biochemical and functional analyses suggest that the role of Nanog in pluripotency is not conserved in all vertebrates, as the Nanog gene is absent in the Xenopus genus (Scerbo et al., 2014) and teleostean Nanog does not support pluripotency during development (Camp et al., 2009; Scerbo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Teleostean Nanog does not support pluripotency during development.
source: Nonetheless, phylogenetic, biochemical and functional analyses suggest that the role of Nanog in pluripotency is not conserved in all vertebrates, as the Nanog gene is absent in the Xenopus genus (Scerbo et al., 2014) and teleostean Nanog does not support pluripotency during development (Camp et al., 2009; Scerbo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ventx transcription factors act as guardians of pluripotency during embryogenesis in Xenopus and zebrafish.
source: Recent analyses on Xenopus and zebrafish embryos suggest that Ventx transcription factors, belonging to the same NK family as Nanog (Scerbo et al., 2014), act as guardians of pluripotency during embryogenesis (Scerbo et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ventx factors integrate the pluripotency network by coordinating and maintaining the activity of Pou-V factors.
source: Ventx factors integrate the pluripotency network by coordinating and maintaining the activity of Pou-V factors (Scerbo et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2004), and by regulating cell response to TGF-β/Smad pathways (Zhu and Kirschner, 2002; Cao et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ventx factors integrate the pluripotency network by regulating cell response to TGF-β/Smad pathways.
source: Ventx factors integrate the pluripotency network by coordinating and maintaining the activity of Pou-V factors (Scerbo et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2004), and by regulating cell response to TGF-β/Smad pathways (Zhu and Kirschner, 2002; Cao et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MEK1 activity can negatively regulate the expression of Nanog and Pou5f1 proteins in vivo.
source: MEK1 activity can negatively regulate both the expression in vivo (Boroviak et al., 2015; Boroviak and Nichols, 2014) and the stability in vitro of Nanog and Pou5f1 proteins (Kim et al., 2014; Spelat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MEK1 activity can negatively regulate the stability of Nanog and Pou5f1 proteins in vitro.
source: MEK1 activity can negatively regulate both the expression in vivo (Boroviak et al., 2015; Boroviak and Nichols, 2014) and the stability in vitro of Nanog and Pou5f1 proteins (Kim et al., 2014; Spelat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Activation of the MAPK ERK1, resulting from phosphorylation by MEK1, occurs at early blastula stages, primarily in the pluripotent cells of the animal and marginal zones.
source: Activation of the MAPK ERK1, resulting from phosphorylation by MEK1, is known to occur at early blastula stages, primarily in the pluripotent cells of the animal and marginal zones (Curran and Grainger, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: FGF-mediated ERK1 activation is necessary for the competence of animal blastula cells to respond to mesoderm and neural inducers.
source: Multiple studies revealed that FGF-mediated ERK1 activation is necessary for the competence of animal blastula cells to respond to mesoderm and neural inducers (Cornell and Kimelman, 1994; Delaune et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mk-MO and Mk-MO ATG both inhibited MEK1 translation.
source: We designed two independent MOs, in the 5'UTR (Mk-MO), and at the ATG (Mk-MO ATG), which both inhibited MEK1 translation and antagonized development (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 1A showing reduced MEK1 protein levels.

claim: Mk-MO and Mk-MO ATG both antagonized development.
source: We designed two independent MOs, in the 5'UTR (Mk-MO), and at the ATG (Mk-MO ATG), which both inhibited MEK1 translation and antagonized development (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1A).
evidence: This is shown by morphological analysis in Figure 1B and marker expression in Figure 1C.

claim: Mk-MO did not up-regulate p53 expression.
source: Mk-MO did not up-regulate p53 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1B), unlike the non-specific response triggered by some MOs in zebrafish embryos (Robu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1B.

claim: A wild-type form of MEK1 from hamster efficiently rescued mesoderm and neural specification in Mk morphant embryos.
source: Importantly, a wild-type form of MEK1 from hamster efficiently rescued mesoderm and neural specification, as well as early morphogenesis, in Mk morphant embryos, indicating that MEK1 knockdown was specific (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1C and D).
evidence: This is shown by WISH analysis in Figure 1D demonstrating restored marker expression.

claim: MEK1 activity was required for the expression of multiple neural and non-neural ectoderm markers.
source: We found that MEK1 activity was required for the expression of multiple neural and non-neural ectoderm, as well as mesoderm markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR and WISH data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2A and B.

claim: MEK1 activity was required for the expression of mesoderm markers.
source: We found that MEK1 activity was required for the expression of multiple neural and non-neural ectoderm, as well as mesoderm markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR and WISH data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2A and B.

claim: MEK1 activity was dispensable for the expression of endoderm markers.
source: In contrast, MEK1 activity was found to be dispensable for the expression of endoderm markers and of immediate-early targets of the BMP and Nodal pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2C and D).
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR and WISH data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2C and D.

claim: MEK1 activity was dispensable for the expression of immediate-early targets of the BMP and Nodal pathways.
source: In contrast, MEK1 activity was found to be dispensable for the expression of endoderm markers and of immediate-early targets of the BMP and Nodal pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2C and D).
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR and WISH data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2C and D.

claim: The expression of the epidermal markers dlx3, gata2 and xk81a1 was reduced in MEK1 morphants, despite the maintained expression of the epidermal inducer bmp4.
source: Interestingly, the expression of the epidermal markers dlx3, gata2 and xk81a1 was reduced in MEK1 morphants, despite the maintained expression of the epidermal inducer bmp4.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data showing reduced epidermal marker expression but maintained bmp4 expression.

claim: Recombinant BMP4, NODAL, and NOGGIN proteins induced efficient expression of epidermal, mesodermal and neural markers, respectively, in wild-type but not in MEK1-depleted cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, recombinant BMP4, NODAL, and NOGGIN proteins induced efficient expression of epidermal, mesodermal and neural markers, respectively, in wild-type but not in MEK1-depleted cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 2A showing differential responses to inducers.

claim: BMP signaling inhibition caused neural induction in wild-type embryos, but not in Mk-MO ATG morphants.
source: Likewise, BMP signaling inhibition, obtained by injection of dominant-negative Smad5 (Marchal et al., 2009), caused neural induction in wild-type embryos, but not in Mk-MO ATG morphants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2–1).
evidence: This is shown by WISH analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2–1.

claim: Multiple epidermal, neural, mesodermal and endodermal markers were induced by BMP4, NOGGIN, low and high doses of NODAL, respectively, in explanted animal ectoderm, but these responses were all abolished in the presence of Mk-MO.
source: Whereas multiple epidermal, neural, mesodermal and endodermal markers were induced by BMP4, NOGGIN, low and high doses of NODAL, respectively, these responses were all abolished in the presence of Mk-MO (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B showing loss of inducer responses in MEK1 morphants.

claim: The expression of pou5f3.1 (oct91), pou5f3.2 (oct25), ventx1 and ventx2 was significantly up-regulated in MEK1-depleted embryos.
source: RT-qPCR analysis on early gastrula embryos revealed that the expression of pou5f3.1 (oct91), pou5f3.2 (oct25), ventx1 and ventx2 was significantly up-regulated in MEK1-depleted embryos, whereas no detectable effect was measured on sox3 and cdh1 (E-cadherin) (Figure 2B)(Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2C.

claim: No detectable effect of MEK1 depletion was measured on sox3 and cdh1 (E-cadherin) expression.
source: RT-qPCR analysis on early gastrula embryos revealed that the expression of pou5f3.1 (oct91), pou5f3.2 (oct25), ventx1 and ventx2 was significantly up-regulated in MEK1-depleted embryos, whereas no detectable effect was measured on sox3 and cdh1 (E-cadherin) (Figure 2B)(Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2C.

claim: ventx2 and pou5f3.2 are initially expressed throughout the pluripotent animal hemisphere and are restricted to non-neural ectoderm and floor plate at late gastrulation, respectively.
source: ventx2 and pou5f3.2 are initially expressed throughout the pluripotent animal hemisphere and are restricted to non-neural ectoderm and floor plate at late gastrulation, respectively, reflecting the progressive engagement of embryonic cells into differentiation.
evidence: This is based on known expression patterns and is supported by WISH data.

claim: ventx2 and pou5f3.2 remained ubiquitously expressed in MEK1 morphants at late gastrula stage.
source: In contrast, these two genes remained ubiquitously expressed in MEK1 morphants at late gastrula stage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 2D.

claim: pou5f3.2 and ventx2 expression failed to be silenced in MEK1 morphants even when morphogenesis was not altered.
source: Likewise, targeted injection of Mk-MO in dorsal or ventral ectoderm confirmed that pou5f3.2 and ventx2 expression failed to be silenced, even when morphogenesis was not altered (Figure 2—figure supplement 2–2A).
evidence: This is shown by WISH analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2–2A.

claim: The maintenance of pou5f3.2 expression in MEK1 morphants was still visible at mid-neurula stage.
source: Strikingly, the maintenance of pou5f3.2 expression in MEK1 morphants was still visible at mid-neurula stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2–2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2–2B.

claim: Gene expression analysis of MEK1-depleted animal ectoderm explants at the end of gastrulation revealed a significantly higher expression of pou5f3.2 and ventx2 with a concomitant reduction of the lineage-restricted markers xk81a1, itln1 and α-tub.
source: Furthermore, gene expression analysis of MEK1-depleted animal ectoderm explants at the end of gastrulation revealed a significantly higher expression of pou5f3.2 and ventx2 with a concomitant reduction of the lineage-restricted markers xk81a1, itln1 and α-tub (Figure 2—figure supplement 2–2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2–2C.

claim: Ventx2 undergoes ubiquitin-mediated degradation in the early gastrula.
source: Consistently, it was shown that Ventx2 undergoes ubiquitin-mediated degradation in the early gastrula (Zhu and Kirschner, 2002), which coincides with the global loss of pluripotency (Snape et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ventx2 proteolysis involves a PEST-destruction motif in its N-terminus, which is regulated by phosphorylation by uncharacterized signaling pathways.
source: Ventx2 proteolysis involves a PEST-destruction motif in its N-terminus, which is regulated by phosphorylation by uncharacterized signaling pathways (Zhu and Kirschner, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The PEST domain is conserved in the Ventx family.
source: Noteworthy, this PEST domain is conserved in the Ventx family (Supplementary file 1)(Supplementary file 4), and one of the two functional serines in the PEST motif of Xenopus Ventx2 is a predicted target of MAPK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by sequence analysis in Supplementary files and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: One of the two functional serines in the PEST motif of Xenopus Ventx2 is a predicted target of MAPK.
source: Noteworthy, this PEST domain is conserved in the Ventx family (Supplementary file 1)(Supplementary file 4), and one of the two functional serines in the PEST motif of Xenopus Ventx2 is a predicted target of MAPK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by in silico analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Western blot analysis of embryos injected with RNA encoding Myc-tagged Ventx2 confirmed the reported degradation after the onset of gastrulation.
source: Western blot analysis of embryos injected with RNA encoding Myc-tagged Ventx2 confirmed the reported degradation after the onset of gastrulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In MEK1 morphants, Ventx2-Myc remained detectable up until mid-gastrula stage.
source: In contrast, in MEK1 morphants, Ventx2-Myc remained detectable up until mid-gastrula stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MEK1 knockdown dramatically increased the number of Ventx2-Myc positive cells at both blastula and gastrula stages.
source: We found that MEK1 knockdown dramatically increased the number of Ventx2-Myc positive cells at both stages, when compared to control (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 3A.

claim: Ventx2-Myc was asymmetrically distributed in daughter cells in control but not in MEK1 morphant embryos.
source: Careful inspection of blastula cells dividing along the animal-vegetal (apical-basal) axis of the tissue revealed that Ventx2-Myc was asymmetrically distributed in daughter cells in control but not in MEK1 morphant embryos (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 3B and C.

claim: A significant fraction of MEK1-depleted cells displayed Ventx2-Myc signal in the membrane cortex at both blastula and gastrula stages.
source: In addition, a significant fraction of MEK1-depleted cells displayed Ventx2-Myc signal in the membrane cortex at both stages analyzed (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy images in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At blastula stage, Ventx2-Myc membrane association was polarized with respect to the plane of the tissue, with a clear basal enrichment.
source: At blastula stage, Ventx2-Myc membrane association was polarized with respect to the plane of the tissue, with a clear basal enrichment (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy images in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 2SAVentx2-Myc was detectable in the nuclei of control cells, similar to Ventx2-Myc in MEK1 morphant cells.
source: As predicted, 2SAVentx2-Myc was detectable in the nuclei of control cells, similar to Ventx2-Myc in MEK1 morphant cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A.

claim: No marked asymmetric distribution of 2SAVentx2-Myc in daughter nuclei of dividing blastula cells was observed.
source: Moreover, no marked asymmetric distribution of 2SAVentx2-Myc in daughter nuclei of dividing blastula cells was observed, suggesting that phosphorylation of the PEST motif is necessary to control Ventx2 asymmetric distribution (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Phosphorylation of the PEST motif is necessary to control Ventx2 asymmetric distribution.
source: Moreover, no marked asymmetric distribution of 2SAVentx2-Myc in daughter nuclei of dividing blastula cells was observed, suggesting that phosphorylation of the PEST motif is necessary to control Ventx2 asymmetric distribution (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutation of the PEST motif abolishes asymmetric distribution.

claim: 2SAVentx2-Myc was detectable in the cortex of injected cells, particularly at gastrula stage, similarly to Ventx2-Myc in MEK-1 deficient cells.
source: Similarly to Ventx2-Myc in MEK-1 deficient cells, 2SAVentx2-Myc was detectable in the cortex of injected cells, particularly at gastrula stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy images in Figure 3A.

claim: Ventx2-Myc localized into the nuclei of blastula cells in prophase and MEK1 depletion did not affect this localization.
source: Ventx2-Myc localized into the nuclei of blastula cells in prophase and MEK1 depletion did not affect this localization.
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy analysis of mitotic phases in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 2SAVentx2-Myc co-localized with chromosomes during prophase.
source: Similarly, 2SAVentx2-Myc co-localized with chromosomes during prophase.
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ventx2 is a phosphomitotic protein.
source: Ventx2 is a phosphomitotic protein (Stukenberg et al., 1997), and it has been proposed that phosphorylation is required for disengagement of transcription factors from chromosomes in metaphase (Stukenberg et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation is required for disengagement of transcription factors from chromosomes in metaphase.
source: Ventx2 is a phosphomitotic protein (Stukenberg et al., 1997), and it has been proposed that phosphorylation is required for disengagement of transcription factors from chromosomes in metaphase (Stukenberg et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ventx2-Myc was no longer associated with metaphasic chromosomes but rather with mitotic spindles.
source: Accordingly, Ventx2-Myc was no longer associated with metaphasic chromosomes but rather with mitotic spindles.
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The change in distribution of Ventx2-Myc from chromosomes to mitotic spindles was independent from MEK1 activity or from the PEST destruction motif.
source: Interestingly, this change in distribution of Ventx2-Myc was independent from MEK1 activity or from the PEST destruction motif.
evidence: This is shown by confocal microscopy analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In control condition, one daughter nucleus contained on average 6.454 fold more Ventx2-Myc than the other daughter nucleus.
source: Quantification of signals intensity revealed that in control condition, one daughter nucleus contained on average 6.454 fold more Ventx2-Myc than the other daughter nucleus (s.e.m. ±0.5479), whereas this difference was significantly dampened in MEK1-deficient cells (mean ratios = 1.092; s.e.m. ±0.0447) and in 2SAVentx2-Myc injected cells (mean ratios = 1.910; s.e.m. ±0.1319)(Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of fluorescence intensity ratios in Figure 3C.

claim: The asymmetry of Ventx2-Myc distribution was significantly dampened in MEK1-deficient cells (mean ratios = 1.092).
source: Quantification of signals intensity revealed that in control condition, one daughter nucleus contained on average 6.454 fold more Ventx2-Myc than the other daughter nucleus (s.e.m. ±0.5479), whereas this difference was significantly dampened in MEK1-deficient cells (mean ratios = 1.092; s.e.m. ±0.0447) and in 2SAVentx2-Myc injected cells (mean ratios = 1.910; s.e.m. ±0.1319)(Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of fluorescence intensity ratios in Figure 3C.

claim: The asymmetry of Ventx2 distribution was significantly dampened in 2SAVentx2-Myc injected cells (mean ratios = 1.910).
source: Quantification of signals intensity revealed that in control condition, one daughter nucleus contained on average 6.454 fold more Ventx2-Myc than the other daughter nucleus (s.e.m. ±0.5479), whereas this difference was significantly dampened in MEK1-deficient cells (mean ratios = 1.092; s.e.m. ±0.0447) and in 2SAVentx2-Myc injected cells (mean ratios = 1.910; s.e.m. ±0.1319)(Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of fluorescence intensity ratios in Figure 3C.

claim: 2SAVentx2-Myc, but not native Ventx2-Myc, caused a markedly high and ectopic expression of pou5f3.2 in late gastrula embryos.
source: Consistent with this idea, 2SAVentx2-Myc, but not native Ventx2-Myc, caused a markedly high and ectopic expression of pou5f3.2 in late gastrula embryos, which was visible up until tailbud stage (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ectopic expression of pou5f3.2 caused by 2SAVentx2-Myc was visible up until tailbud stage.
source: Consistent with this idea, 2SAVentx2-Myc, but not native Ventx2-Myc, caused a markedly high and ectopic expression of pou5f3.2 in late gastrula embryos, which was visible up until tailbud stage (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 2SAVentx2-Myc but not Ventx2-Myc could counteract the conversion of ectoderm to mesoderm in response to a constitutively active form of MEK1.
source: Furthermore, we found that 2SAVentx2-Myc but not Ventx2-Myc could counteract the conversion of ectoderm to mesoderm in response to a constitutively active form of MEK1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 4B showing differential t/bra expression.

claim: 2SAVentx2-Myc has become resistant to degradation induced by MEK1.
source: This result suggests that 2SAVentx2-Myc has become resistant to degradation induced by MEK1 and can efficiently maintain pluripotency and antagonize commitment in the presence of active MEK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 2SAVentx2-Myc can counteract CA-MEK1 activity.

claim: 2SAVentx2-Myc can efficiently maintain pluripotency and antagonize commitment in the presence of active MEK1.
source: This result suggests that 2SAVentx2-Myc has become resistant to degradation induced by MEK1 and can efficiently maintain pluripotency and antagonize commitment in the presence of active MEK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 2SAVentx2-Myc can counteract CA-MEK1 activity and maintain pou5f3.2 expression.

claim: Ventx2 MO injection caused the down-regulation of ventx1 and ventx3 expression.
source: RT-qPCR and in situ hybridization analyses revealed that Ventx2 MO injection caused the down-regulation of ventx1 and ventx3 expression, suggesting that a large part of Ventx activity is missing in such embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR and WISH data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: A large part of Ventx activity is missing in Ventx2 morphant embryos.
source: RT-qPCR and in situ hybridization analyses revealed that Ventx2 MO injection caused the down-regulation of ventx1 and ventx3 expression, suggesting that a large part of Ventx activity is missing in such embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is inferred from the down-regulation of other Ventx family members.

claim: MEK1-Ventx2 double morphant cells regained the competence to respond to exogenous inducers and express epidermal, neural, mesodermal and endodermal markers.
source: As predicted, MEK1-Ventx2 double morphant cells regained the competence to respond to exogenous inducers and thus to express epidermal, neural, mesodermal and endodermal markers in response to BMP4, NOGGIN, low and high doses of NODAL, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 4C showing restored marker expression in response to inducers.

claim: The expression of the lineage-restricted markers foxd5, gsc, t/bra, and xk81a1 was rescued in MEK1-Ventx2 double morphant embryos.
source: Furthermore, the expression of the lineage-restricted markers foxd5, gsc, t/bra, and xk81a1 was rescued in MEK1-Ventx2 double morphant embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The sustained expression of pou5f3.2 caused by MEK1 depletion was counteracted by concomitant Ventx2 knockdown.
source: Conversely, the sustained expression of pou5f3.2 caused by MEK1 depletion was counteracted by concomitant Ventx2 knockdown (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by WISH analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: Morphogenesis and axis formation was partially restored in MEK1-Ventx2 double morphant embryos.
source: Finally, morphogenesis and axis formation was also partially restored in MEK1-Ventx2 double morphant embryos (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological scoring in Figure 4E.

claim: MEK1 and Ventx2 functionally interact during the transition of pluripotent cells from refractory to responsive states.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that MEK1 and Ventx2 functionally interact during the transition of pluripotent cells from refractory to responsive states.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of differentiation competence in double morphants.

claim: This is the first reported regulatory mechanism that correlates the asymmetric distribution and stability of a transcription factor with cell pluripotency in vertebrate embryos.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first reported regulatory mechanism that correlates the asymmetric distribution and stability of a transcription factor with cell pluripotency in vertebrate embryos.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The rescue of cell differentiation in double MEK1/Ventx2 morphants suggests that endogenous Ventx2 is under the same control as exogenous tagged Ventx2.
source: Although we used exogenous Ventx2 tagged proteins to reveal this mechanism, the rescue of cell differentiation in double MEK1/Ventx2 morphants suggests that endogenous Ventx2 is under the same control.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional rescue experiments.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin pathway orients asymmetric cell division of mESCs and generates unequal distribution of pluripotency factors, which impacts on cell potency in vitro.
source: Our data are consistent with a recent finding, whereby the Wnt/β-catenin pathway orients asymmetric cell division of mESCs and generates unequal distribution of pluripotency factors, which impacts on cell potency in vitro (Habib et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ventx2 phosphorylation in the PEST motif is required for ubiquitination and degradation.
source: Ventx2 phosphorylation in the PEST motif was shown to be required for ubiquitination and degradation (Zhu and Kirschner, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The asymmetric distribution of Ventx2 during mitosis and proteasome activity may be related.
source: Thus, our observation that mutation of the Ventx2 PEST motif prevents unequal distribution in daughter nuclei suggests that the asymmetric distribution of Ventx2 during mitosis and proteasome activity may be related.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PEST mutation affects asymmetric distribution.

claim: MEK1 may act directly or through MAPK to phosphorylate the Ventx2 PEST motif and promote Ventx2 proteolysis.
source: In the simplest scenario, MEK1 may act directly or through MAPK to phosphorylate the Ventx2 PEST motif and promote Ventx2 proteolysis.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the data and known MAPK functions.

claim: MAPK ERK1 is a known regulator of pluripotency factor stability in vitro.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the MAPK ERK1 is a known regulator of pluripotency factor stability in vitro (Spelat et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2014), and MAPK is predicted to phosphorylate one of the key serine residues in the Ventx2 PEST domain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MEK1 depletion caused stronger responses than 2SAVentx2 injection.
source: We note, however, that MEK1 depletion caused stronger responses than 2SAVentx2 injection, suggesting that MEK1 regulates pluripotency through additional residues in Ventx2 and/or through additional effectors.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of phenotypic severity.

claim: MEK1 regulates pluripotency through additional residues in Ventx2 and/or through additional effectors.
source: We note, however, that MEK1 depletion caused stronger responses than 2SAVentx2 injection, suggesting that MEK1 regulates pluripotency through additional residues in Ventx2 and/or through additional effectors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MEK1 depletion has stronger effects than PEST mutation.

claim: The BMP signal mediator Smad1 was found to be asymmetrically distributed during somatic cell division, when marked for degradation by MAPK.
source: Interestingly, the BMP signal mediator Smad1 was also found to be asymmetrically distributed during somatic cell division, when marked for degradation by MAPK (Fuentealba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation by MAPK triggers a subsequent phosphorylation event by GSK3, followed by polyubiquitinylation and proteosomal degradation of activated Smad1, leading to BMP signal termination.
source: There, phosphorylation by MAPK triggers a subsequent phosphorylation event by GSK3, followed by polyubiquitinylation and proteosomal degradation of activated Smad1, leading to BMP signal termination.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature (Fuentealba et al., 2008).

claim: There is no evidence of GSK3 involvement in the repression of pluripotency genes and in Ventx2 degradation.
source: In contrast, we did not find evidence of GSK3 involvement in the repression of pluripotency genes and in Ventx2 degradation (Supplementary file 1), consistent with previous data (Zhu and Kirschner, 2002).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and citation to published literature.

claim: MEK1 may trigger important proteolytic events in early embryos, independently of GSK3.
source: Thus, MEK1 may trigger important proteolytic events in early embryos, independently of GSK3.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of GSK3 involvement in Ventx2 degradation.

claim: ERK1 antagonizes the polarized PAR-1 kinase during asymmetric cell divisions of the early C. elegans embryo.
source: For instance, ERK1 was shown to antagonize the polarized PAR-1 kinase during asymmetric cell divisions of the early C. elegans embryo (Spilker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Asymmetric proteasome segregation controls polarized degradation of the phosphorylated transcription factor T-bet during T lymphocyte division.
source: Also related to this idea, asymmetric proteasome segregation was shown to control polarized degradation of the phosphorylated transcription factor T-bet during T lymphocyte division (Chang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A balance between the PAR-1 kinase and PP2A phosphatase controls the state of PAR-3 phosphorylation and thus the polarity of dividing embryonic neuroblasts in Drosophila.
source: Such a balance between the PAR-1 kinase and PP2A phosphatase was shown to control the state of PAR-3 phosphorylation and thus the polarity of dividing embryonic neuroblasts in Drosophila (Krahn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: MEK1 actively prevents membrane association of Ventx2.
source: This localization was not apparent in control cells, suggesting that it does not simply reflect the over-abundance of Ventx2 protein due to synthetic RNA injection. Rather, this suggests that MEK1 actively prevents membrane association of Ventx2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ventx2 localizes to membranes in MEK1 morphants but not in controls.

claim: The basal membrane cortex may represent a storage compartment for Ventx2 protein.
source: As stabilized 2SAVentx2 also localized at membranes, this territory may represent a storage compartment for Ventx2 protein.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed membrane localization.

claim: Pou5f1 and Pou5f3 proteins localize at the cell membrane both in mESCs and in Xenopus animal pole cells, where they form a complex with E-cadherin and β-catenin.
source: In relevance to our observations, it was reported that Pou5f1 and Pou5f3 proteins localize at the cell membrane both in mESCs and in Xenopus animal pole cells, where they form a complex with E-cadherin and β-catenin (Livigni et al., 2013; Faunes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ventx2 can physically interact with Pou5f3 proteins.
source: Since Ventx2 can physically interact with Pou5f3 proteins (Cao et al., 2004), we speculate that MEK1 may be required to destabilize the interaction between Ventx2 and Pou5f3, not only in the nucleus but also at the membrane, further enhancing the competence of embryonic cells to exit pluripotency.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: MEK1 may be required to destabilize the interaction between Ventx2 and Pou5f3, not only in the nucleus but also at the membrane.
source: Since Ventx2 can physically interact with Pou5f3 proteins (Cao et al., 2004), we speculate that MEK1 may be required to destabilize the interaction between Ventx2 and Pou5f3, not only in the nucleus but also at the membrane, further enhancing the competence of embryonic cells to exit pluripotency.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known protein interactions and observed localizations.

claim: Ventx2 is a bona fide marker of pluripotency during Xenopus embryogenesis.
source: Ventx2 is a bona fide marker of pluripotency during Xenopus embryogenesis (Scerbo et al., 2012; Buitrago-Delgado et al., 2015), and the above data indicate that its activity must be inhibited for cells to engage into differentiation pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ventx2 activity must be inhibited for cells to engage into differentiation pathways.
source: Ventx2 is a bona fide marker of pluripotency during Xenopus embryogenesis (Scerbo et al., 2012; Buitrago-Delgado et al., 2015), and the above data indicate that its activity must be inhibited for cells to engage into differentiation pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Ventx2 clearance is necessary for differentiation.

claim: A unique VENTX gene is present in human.
source: This may reflect the absence of Ventx orthologs in the rodent genus, although a unique VENTX gene is present in human (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis presented in supplementary data.

claim: A Ventx gene appeared at the base of gnathostome evolution, and its prototypical genomic locus has not changed for 450 My.
source: Phylogenetic and synteny analyses suggest that a Ventx gene appeared at the base of gnathostome evolution, and its prototypical genomic locus has not changed for 450 My (Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and synteny analyses presented in supplementary data.

claim: Human VENTX is the ortholog of Xenopus, birds, sauropside and coelacanth Ventx2.
source: Human VENTX is the ortholog of Xenopus, birds, sauropside and coelacanth Ventx2 (Supplementary files 2 and 4).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis presented in supplementary data.

claim: A recent study reported a 6-fold up-regulation of VENTX (higher than NANOG, PRDM14, POU5F1 and SOX2) in naive hESCs compared to conventional hESCs.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reported a 6-fold up-regulation of VENTX (higher than NANOG, PRDM14, POU5F1 and SOX2) in naive hESCs compared to conventional hESCs (Theunissen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Naive hESCs were obtained in the presence of inhibitors of five kinases, including MEK1.
source: In this study, naive hESCs were obtained in the presence of inhibitors of five kinases, including MEK1, suggesting that repression of VENTX by MEK1 may be conserved in human pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature (Theunissen et al., 2014).

claim: Repression of VENTX by MEK1 may be conserved in human pluripotent cells.
source: In this study, naive hESCs were obtained in the presence of inhibitors of five kinases, including MEK1, suggesting that repression of VENTX by MEK1 may be conserved in human pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that VENTX is upregulated when MEK1 is inhibited in human cells.

claim: VENTX is absent in rodents.
source: As VENTX is absent in rodents, we propose that Xenopus represents an appropriate and powerful model to undertake comparative approaches with human and shed light on the control mechanisms of pluripotency in vivo and at single cell level.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Xenopus represents an appropriate and powerful model to undertake comparative approaches with human to study pluripotency control mechanisms.
source: As VENTX is absent in rodents, we propose that Xenopus represents an appropriate and powerful model to undertake comparative approaches with human and shed light on the control mechanisms of pluripotency in vivo and at single cell level.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the presence of VENTX in both Xenopus and human but not in rodents.

claim: Asymmetric clearance of pluripotency regulators may represent an important mechanism to ensure the progressive assembly of primitive embryonic tissues.
source: We suggest that asymmetric clearance of pluripotency regulators may represent an important mechanism to ensure the progressive assembly of primitive embryonic tissues.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.
